slides.notes: [10:42–10:47] The point of this slide is ownership. AI in a plant is 80% this asset and 20% algorithm, and the asset is already bought, installed and collecting. slides.title: The one idea of the day
slides.subtitle: Everything called 'AI' in this course is one subtraction, dressed four ways
slides.notes: [10:53–11:00] Slow down here — this is THE slide. Walk the four steps with the bearing: we measured 74.2; the model, given today's load, ambient and cooling water, expected 71.9; the residual is +2.3; and a residual that stays big and positive for days is a machine asking for attention. Say the sentence the day keeps returning to: a flat residual means a healthy machine, whatever the weather is doing. Every algorithm this afternoon — k-NN, networks, PCA — is just a different way of computing step two.
steps: Measure
What the sensor reads now: 74.2 °C on the DE bearing.
Expect
What history says the reading SHOULD be for this load, ambient and cooling-water temperature: 71.9 °C.
Subtract
Residual = actual − expected = +2.3 °C. The weather and the duty have been removed; what is left is the machine.
Decide
A residual that stays outside its band for days is evidence. Evidence goes to a person, who decides.
slides.punch: Expected − actual = the residual. Flat residual = healthy machine, whatever the weather.

slides.title: Three ways machines learn
slides.subtitle: Ninety seconds of vocabulary, in plant language, then never again
slides.notes: [11:09–11:11] Do not linger — this is vocabulary, not theory. One plant example each: supervised is 'predict bearing temperature from load and ambient'; unsupervised is 'group this year into operating regimes nobody named'; reinforcement is 'learn a control policy by trial' — and say plainly that reinforcement learning belongs nowhere near a live unit today. Then the last row: nearly everything in this course is supervised learning of an expected value. The vendor word-cloud collapses to one idea.
items: Supervised
Learn a mapping from examples with answers: given load, ambient and CW temperature, predict what this bearing should read.
Unsupervised
Find structure without answers: cluster a year of operation into regimes — start-up, low load, summer full load — nobody labelled.
Reinforcement
Learn actions by trial and reward. Powerful, and not for live plant — nothing today, and nothing this year, should use it on a unit.
What today uses
Almost everything in this course is supervised learning of an expected value, plus honest subtraction. Keep the vocabulary that small.

slides.title: The simplest model that works
slides.subtitle: k-nearest neighbours: the residual, computed by memory instead of mathematics
slides.notes: [11:11–11:15] Before any network: the dumbest honest model. To know what the bearing should read now, find the 12 most similar past hours — similar load, similar ambient, similar cooling water — and average what the bearing read then. That average IS the expected value; subtract and you have a residual. No training, no weights, fully explainable: 'you ran like this on these 12 days, and you were cooler then.' Most commercial condition-monitoring products are exactly this with better packaging. Module 1 shows it in 3-D — homework.
steps: Take now
This hour's load, ambient and cooling-water temperature — the operating point.
Search history
Find the 12 most similar healthy hours in the year. Similarity is just distance.
Average them
What the bearing read on those 12 hours, averaged, is the expected value.
Subtract
Actual minus expected — the residual again. A lookup table beat the mystique.
slides.punch: Most commercial monitoring systems are this slide, well packaged. Keep that as your baseline.

slides.title: Lab — Theatre Module 3 · Gradient descent
slides.subtitle: Twelve minutes: fit a model by rolling a ball downhill, and break it yourself
slides.notes: [LAB] [11:15–11:27] Hand over to the phones. The loss surface is drawn as terrain: every position is a candidate model, height is how wrong it is, and training is a ball rolling downhill. The one thing everyone must do is break it: push the learning rate up until the ball overshoots the valley and diverges. Seeing divergence beats reading about it. Walk the room; ask people what their smallest reliable step size was. Close with: every model today — including the 163-dial network next — is fitted by exactly this ball.

lab.name: Gradient descent — how a model is actually fitted
do: Open the Theatre from the landing page; pick Module 3
Play the acts: the terrain, the ball, the step size
Drag the learning rate UP until training visibly diverges
Find the largest step that still converges — that tension is real
see: The loss falling fast, then flattening — the shape of all training
Too large a step overshooting the valley and climbing the far wall
The same loss curve you will meet again in the Model Builder
lab.why: Training is not mystical: it is descent on an error surface. Once you have personally made it diverge, no vendor can hand-wave 'the model learns' past you.

slides.title: What 'training' means, in one line
slides.subtitle: The ball, written as algebra — the only equation the day insists on
slides.notes: [11:27–11:30] Freeze the lab and put the line up. w is one dial; the gradient is that dial's share of the blame for the current error; eta is the step size they just tuned by hand. Training is this line, applied to every dial, over every training hour, many times. Say it in plant words: turn each dial a little against its share of the blame, repeat until the error stops falling. This exact line reappears in the Model Builder after lunch, printed live with their model's own numbers.

left.label: The rule
left.detail: One dial at a time: move each weight a small step against its own contribution to the error. η is the step size you just tuned by hand in Module 3.

right.label: In plant words
right.detail: The error at the output is divided among the dials by the chain rule; each dial moves against its share. Repeat over every hour of history until the error stops falling.

slides.punch: You will see this exact line again after lunch, running live with your own model's numbers.

slides.title: What you just tapped
slides.subtitle: One neuron of the network, exactly as the panel showed it
slides.notes: [11:45–11:48] Mirror the phone on the projector so the room and the slide agree. This is neuron 1 of hidden layer 1 at the specimen hour: three of its eight weighted inputs, the bias, the sum, and tanh of the sum. Read it aloud once: multiply, add, squash — that is the entire operation of a neuron, and a 'layer' is seventeen of these in a row. The numbers are the REAL trained weights from the module, not an illustration.
slides.punch: Multiply, add, squash. A 'layer' is seventeen of these. That is the whole mystery.

slides.title: The backward pass, on the same hour
slides.subtitle: Where the weights come from — the chain rule, sharing out the blame
slides.notes: [11:48–11:53] The forward pass answered; now the error runs backwards. Walk the four steps with the module's own numbers on screen. Then the detail worth a minute: the derivative of tanh is 1 − a². The saturated neuron they found — output pinned at ±1 — has derivative near zero, so its dials barely move however wrong the answer is. It has stopped learning. That is the vanishing gradient, seen on their own phone rather than asserted from a slide.
steps: Error at the output
δ = 2(ŷ − y): how wrong, and in which direction, on this hour.
Share the blame
The chain rule passes δ backwards; each neuron receives exactly its share.
Gradient per dial
∂L/∂w = δ × input. A dial fed by a big input carries more of the blame.
Update
w ← w − η·∂L/∂w — Module 3's line, applied 163 times, once per dial.
slides.punch: tanh′ = 1 − a². A neuron pinned at ±1 has stopped learning — you found one yourself.

slides.title: Why the bend matters
slides.subtitle: Remove every activation and the whole stack collapses
slides.notes: [11:53–11:56] The squash is not decoration. A stack of purely linear layers — any depth — multiplies out to ONE linear map: a straight line, however many millions of weights. The bend at each neuron is what lets the network represent a curve. Plant the seed for Block 3: there is a real curve waiting — a lube-oil cooler that runs out of approach above its design cooling-water temperature — and a straight-line model fitted to winter will be confidently wrong about it all summer.

left.label: Without activations
left.detail: Ten linear layers multiply out to a single linear regression. Depth adds nothing — the stack collapses.

right.label: With a bend at each neuron
right.detail: Enough bent units approximate any well-behaved relationship — including the cooler knee you will meet after this block.

slides.punch: Hold that thought: Block 3 has a real knee, and a straight line will lie about it.

slides.title: The first sanity check on any model
slides.subtitle: Sensitivity: what the network actually leans on, at the current operating point
slides.notes: [11:56–11:59] Module 4 computes this live by running the backward pass one step further, to the inputs: how many degrees the prediction moves per unit of each tag. Load and ambient dominate — exactly as the physics says they should. That agreement is the check. Give the room the rule: on ANY supplied model, ask for this table first, and if the biggest sensitivity is a tag with no physical route to the target, the model has learned a coincidence of the training window and will betray you the first time the coincidence breaks.

slides.title: What a neural network is — and is not
slides.subtitle: The honest datasheet, before anyone gets romantic
slides.notes: [11:59–12:02] Read the pairs briskly and let the last row land hard: for one bearing on one fan, a network this size is usually the WRONG tool — k-NN and PCA are simpler, need less data and fail more visibly. Networks earn their keep where the relationship is strongly non-linear and history is long: combustion, mill throughput, load-following steam temperatures. Choosing the smallest model that works is an engineering decision, not a fashion decision — that sentence is the block's takeaway for anyone who ever meets a vendor.

slides.title: The regimes nobody labelled
slides.subtitle: Module 6 in one slide — unsupervised learning as an operating-mode detector
slides.notes: [12:02–12:04] One breath on k-means, because it returns in Block 4: give the algorithm a year of operation and no labels at all, and it discovers the unit's operating regimes by itself — start-up, low load, summer full load. Why it matters: a single expected-value model straddling all regimes is mediocre in every one of them. Real monitoring systems fit one model per regime, and this is the machine that finds the regimes. Module 6 is homework on the same URL.

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: Why synthetic data at all
slides.subtitle: A teaching fault needs a birthday — real historians never confess one
slides.notes: [12:05–12:09] Be direct about the method, because honesty here buys trust all day. Real plant data never tells you the true onset day of a fault, so you can never mark a model's homework with it. The labs therefore run on a synthetic year: generated from a physical model, with the fault injected on a KNOWN day. The machine data is synthetic; the economics around it are from our June bill. Synthetic is not fake — it is the only data against which a detection claim can be checked exactly.

left.label: A real historian export
left.detail: When did the degradation truly begin? Real data never says — so 'we detected it 40 days early' can never be verified against truth.

right.label: The synthetic year in today's labs
right.detail: Fault injected on a known day, growing by a known law. Every detection claim today is marked against this answer key, in front of you.

slides.punch: Synthetic data is not fake data. It is the only data with an answer key.

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: How the year is built
slides.subtitle: Three context signals, each with the physics that makes winter unlike May
slides.notes: [12:09–12:14] Walk the three rows — this generator is worth two minutes because everything after lunch runs on it. Load is mean-reverting around 80% with night and Sunday dips. Ambient is the important one: monthly means that climb to a May peak of 33.5 °C and then DROP when the monsoon arrives — a shape no sine wave can make, and precisely why a model fitted to one season mis-predicts another. Cooling water follows air with about nine days of lag, because a basin has thermal inertia. Noise on top of all of it.

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: How a fault is injected
slides.subtitle: Severity grows by a power law — and the first third produces almost nothing
slides.notes: [12:14–12:18] The fault law: severity = ((t − onset)/ttf)^shape. For the fan, onset day 200, 110 days to failure, shape 1.7. Look at the curve's belly: 30 days in, severity is 11%; at half life it is still around a third. The residual it produces (orange) follows the same convexity. This single curve answers every 'why did detection take so long' question for the rest of the day — the early fault is genuinely quiet, and nobody catches by eyeball what has not yet made a signal.

Days of warning are therefore cheap early and expensive late

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: The knee — one line of physics
slides.subtitle: Why this dataset must be a year long, in a single equation
slides.notes: [12:18–12:22] The lube-oil cooler is sized for a design cooling-water temperature of 27.5 °C. Below it, oil temperature tracks ambient almost linearly. Above it the cooler runs out of approach, and the generator adds 1.35 × (CW − 27.5)^1.45 — a knee. Fit a straight line to January and February, when CW sits at 19–22 °C, and it extrapolates confidently into May and is badly wrong, because it never saw the knee exist. This is the bend from Block 2, now with a nameplate on it — and in twenty minutes everyone reproduces the failure personally.

left.label: Below 27.5 °C cooling water
left.detail: Oil outlet tracks ambient almost perfectly. A straight-line model fitted here looks excellent — on winter.

right.label: Above 27.5 °C
right.detail: The cooler runs out of approach and oil temperature climbs far faster than the water. Winter models never learned this term exists.

slides.punch: Fit winter, extrapolate May, alarm all summer. You will do exactly this, on purpose, in 20 minutes.

slides.subtitle: Train on days 0–45 and the model is confidently wrong all summer
slides.notes: [12:49–12:52] The room has just done this. The winter model looks BETTER on its own window — tighter sigma, lovely fit — and then runs +2.4 °C wrong on average through the pre-monsoon, four times its own alert band, nineteen times worse than the season-spanning model. It never met the knee. Name the lesson while their thumbs are still on it: a model that has not seen a season does not know the season exists, and no amount of architecture fixes a training window.

left.label: Winter window, judged on winter
left.detail: Fits January beautifully — tighter than the honest model. Every bad model looks good on its own training data.

right.label: Same model, meeting May
right.detail: Runs +2.4 °C wrong on average before any fault exists — 19× worse than the season-spanning window. It never saw the knee.

slides.punch: You just caused seasonal overfitting, on purpose, 90 seconds after being warned about it.

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: Experiment 3 — the cardinal sin
slides.subtitle: Let the training window touch the fault, and the model learns the fault is normal
slides.notes: [12:52–12:55] Two numbers from their own phones: end the window at day 300 — inside the degradation — and the advisory slides from day 255 to day 315, sixty days of warning gone. End it at day 330 and the advisory never comes at all. Nothing on the loss curve warns you; the model is perfectly happy. This is the single most common way real condition-monitoring programmes die, and the defence is procedural, not clever: the training window ends before the period you intend to judge.

left.label: Window 0–300 — touches the fault
left.detail: 60 days of warning lost. The model absorbed the early degradation as 'normal' and raised its own alert band to match.

right.label: Window 0–330 — swallows the fault
right.detail: The model now expects the fault. The residual stays inside the band while the machine walks to failure.

slides.punch: Train on the fault and the model learns the fault is normal. Nothing on the loss curve tells you.

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: Experiment 4 — buy back 25 days with one tag
slides.subtitle: The engineer's tag beats the data scientist's architecture
slides.notes: [12:55–12:58] Last experiment: tick the lube-oil cooler outlet temperature into the inputs and retrain. Sigma collapses from 2.05 to 0.60 °C — the knee is now explained, the band tightens from ±8.2 to ±2.4 — and the advisory moves from day 255 to day 230. Twenty-five days of warning, bought by knowing WHERE the failure starts. No layer count achieves this. Input choice beats architecture, which means the person who knows the plant beats the person who knows the library.

left.label: Duty + weather only
left.detail: σ 2.05 °C, band ±8.2. The model cannot see the cooler, so the knee sits inside its error — as band width.

right.label: + lube-oil cooler outlet
right.detail: σ 0.60 °C, band ±2.4. The mechanism tag explains the knee, the band closes, and 25 days of warning appear.

slides.punch: Input choice beats architecture. The engineer who knows the plant wins.

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: Where the alert band actually comes from
slides.subtitle: σ is the model's ignorance, not the instrument's noise
slides.notes: [12:58–13:00] One more reading of the same numbers, because it changes how people argue with vendors. The default model's σ of 2.05 °C splits: only 0.89 °C is hour-to-hour sensor noise; the remaining 1.8 °C is structure the model fails to explain — mostly the knee. The alarm band is therefore a property of the MODEL, not the machine: improve the model and the band narrows, and detection days appear out of nowhere. The Builder prints this split on every run. Break for lunch on time.

left.label: Irreducible sensor noise
left.detail: Measured from hour-to-hour differences. No model, however clever, removes this floor.

right.label: The model's own ignorance
right.detail: Structure the inputs cannot explain — mostly the knee. This part is yours to remove, and Experiment 4 just removed it.

slides.punch: The alarm band is a property of the model, not the machine. Lunch — leave the Builder open.

slides.block: 3 · Data synthesis and the Model Builder
slides.title: Three rules for a training window
slides.subtitle: Everything Block 3 taught, as procedure — laminate this
slides.notes: [13:45–13:48] Reconvene after lunch by compressing the morning into procedure. Three rules plus the standing one: span the seasons, end before the period you judge, feed the model duty rather than symptoms — and retrain after any overhaul, because maintenance legitimately changes what 'normal' is. These four lines are the difference between the honest day-255 model and the silent day-330 one, and they cost nothing but discipline. Then pivot: the afternoon takes this discipline to a full maintenance programme.
steps: Span the seasons
A window that has not met May does not know May exists. One full year, minimum, in this climate.
End before the fault
The window must end before the period you intend to judge — always, procedurally, no exceptions.
Duty in, symptoms out
Inputs are what drives the machine (load, ambient, CW). A symptom tag as input teaches the model to expect the fault.
Retrain after overhaul
Maintenance changes 'normal'. A model that remembers the old bearing alarms on the new one.
slides.punch: The training window is a decision. Make it deliberately, and write it down.

slides.title: From one model to a programme
slides.subtitle: The eight stages of the PdM simulator — and where programmes actually die
slides.notes: [13:48–13:52] The morning built stage 6 and nothing else. A predictive maintenance PROGRAMME is all eight stages, and the uncomfortable truth is that most failures happen in stages 1–4 — before any algorithm exists. Wrong failure mode, missing sensor, dead data, unexamined quality: no model recovers from these. The simulator the room is about to drive walks all eight in order, on five different machines, and the afternoon follows its structure.

right: 06 · Model training — the morning's whole story

The glamour lives here; the leverage lives on the left
slides.punch: Most PdM programmes die in stages 1–4, before any AI exists to blame.

slides.subtitle: The simulator's cases — synthetic datasets, real failure physics
slides.notes: [13:52–13:55] Introduce the cast. Five machines, each with a genuine failure mode, realistic instrumentation gaps, and a synthetic year with a known fault day — say the synthetic part out loud again; the honesty is a feature. The ID fan is today's guided case; the other four run the same eight stages and are homework. Each case also carries a deliberate trap — a sensor that is not fitted, a tag that would leak the answer — because real programmes meet exactly these.

slides.title: Stage 1 — name the failure mode
slides.subtitle: A predictive model with no named failure mode is a dashboard
slides.notes: [13:55–13:58] Before any data: what exactly are we trying to catch? For the fan the chain is specific — cooling-water side of the lube-oil cooler fouls, oil runs hot, the film thins, the babbitt wipes, and the machine trips at 100 °C metal temperature. Walk the chain and note that each link suggests its own instrument. A programme that skips this stage produces dashboards: colourful, comprehensive, and incapable of answering 'what would we have caught, and when?'

Cooling-water side of the oil cooler fouls — slowly, over months.

Failure
Trip — or a wiped bearing and a forced outage measured in days.
slides.punch: Name the failure mode first. Every link in the chain tells you what to measure.

The lesson from Experiment 4 applies in reverse: the mechanism tag is worth 25 days of warning, so a ₹50,000 sensor can outperform a ₹50 lakh analytics platform. Ask the room which tags their own worst actor is missing; every unit has this list.

slides.title: Stage 4 — the data-quality gates
slides.subtitle: Five ways the data lies before any model sees it
slides.notes: [14:19–14:23] Each of these was injectable in the lab they just ran. Walk them quickly — the room has now SEEN a flatlined sensor make the machine look immortal. The gate discipline: every tag gets a quality profile before it is allowed near training — freeze detection, gap census, range checks, timestamp audit. It is unglamorous, it is an AE-level responsibility, and it decides more than the model does.
warnings: Flatline
A frozen sensor reads one value for weeks. A model trained on it learns the tag is a constant — and misses everything.
Gaps & timeouts
'I/O Timeout' and missing hours, silently zero-filled, teach the model the machine periodically freezes solid.
Compression
Historian dead-banding smooths real variation away; the noise floor is understated and every band is too tight.
Calibration drift
A sensor drifting 2 °C looks exactly like a machine drifting 2 °C — until the twin tag disagrees.
Clock skew
Tags stamped by different systems minutes apart smear every relationship the model must learn.
slides.never: Never train on: unprofiled tags · zero-filled gaps · a window containing the fault · another unit's data unchecked

slides.title: Stage 5 — features are engineering
slides.subtitle: What to hand the model, and the traps that look helpful
slides.notes: [14:23–14:27] Features are where plant knowledge enters. The good list: load-normalised temperature, the DE-minus-NDE difference that kills common-mode drift AND separates sensor fault from machine fault in one subtraction, the oil ΔT across the cooler pointing at the mechanism, seven-day slopes. The traps look innocent: hour-of-day correlates with everything and means nothing; day-number ENCODES the answer for a synthetic fault; and any symptom tag as an input is Experiment 4's negative-residual problem waiting to misdirect an investigation.

Oil ΔT across the cooler — the mechanism, directly
7-day rolling mean and slope — shift noise suppressed
Duty tags: current, flow, ambient — 'expected' lives here
right: Hour of day — correlates with everything, means nothing
Day number — encodes the answer outright; leakage
Any symptom tag as an input — teaches the model the fault
The twin bearing as input — model copies it and learns nothing
Kitchen-sink features — more inputs, more coincidences
slides.punch: DE − NDE is the 30-second triage: a sensor fault moves alone, a machine fault moves both.

slides.title: Stage 6 — model families, honestly
slides.subtitle: Three ways to compute 'expected' — all of them the same idea
slides.notes: [14:27–14:30] Thirty seconds each, because the room has already met two from the inside. k-NN: memory, no training, fully explainable, what most commercial systems actually run. Regression/networks: the morning's story, interpretable at this size. Autoencoders: compress-and-reconstruct, reconstruction error as the residual — PCA's idea with bends. Then the de-mystifier: all three produce an expected value and a residual. The family matters less than the window, the inputs and the validation — which is why those got the morning and this gets a slide.
cards: k-NN similarity
No training, fully explainable, robust. What most commercial CM systems really run under the paint.
Regression / small network
The morning's entire story. Interpretable at 31–163 parameters; retrain in seconds.
Autoencoder
Compress and reconstruct; the reconstruction error is the residual. PCA with bends — for many tags at once.
All of them
Produce expected − actual. Window, inputs and validation decide success; the family mostly decides the brochure.
slides.punch: Every family computes the same subtraction. Spend your judgement on windows and inputs, not brand names.

slides.title: Stage 7 — validation that means something
slides.subtitle: The alert budget: how many pages a year buys how many days of warning
slides.notes: [14:30–14:34] Validation is not a accuracy percentage — it is an alert budget. Read the table: at 4σ held 72 hours, one episode a year and 55 days of warning; loosen to 2σ/24h and warning improves marginally while episodes explode into the dozens — and a control room ignores the 41st false page. The budget is a MANAGEMENT decision: how many investigations a month will maintenance actually staff? Pick that number first, then set σ and persistence to spend it.

slides.title: The sister-machine check
slides.subtitle: The negative control every claimed detection must pass
slides.notes: [14:34–14:37] The simulator runs the same trained model on fan B — identical duty, healthy all year, judged by its own threshold. Result: zero episodes. That is the negative control: if the model alarms on the healthy twin, it learned the weather, not the fault. And the small print that catches real vendors: the threshold must come from the sister's own quiet period — apply machine A's band to machine B and the nuisance rate is silently faked to zero. Ask for the sister-machine run in every vendor demonstration.

left.detail: Advisory day 255, sustained, single episode. The detection claim.

right.label: Fan B — healthy twin, own threshold
right.detail: Same model, same year, zero alarms. If this number is not zero, the model learned the season — not the fault.

slides.punch: No sister-machine run, no belief. Ask for it in every vendor demo.

slides.title: Remaining useful life — a band, not a date
slides.subtitle: The difference between astrology and engineering
slides.notes: [14:37–14:40] When the advisory fires, the next question is always 'how long?' — and a point estimate is the wrong answer to give a planning meeting. Degradation rates vary with load and coal; the honest output is a distribution: 90% confident it survives past the next planned outage window, 10% it does not. Planning can act on a band — advance a window, stage spares, derate on hot afternoons. Nobody can act on a fictional date except by pretending. SIM-5 in the Simulation Lab does the full RUL exercise; homework.

left.label: What gets asked for
left.detail: A single confident date. It will be wrong, it will be remembered, and it will cost the programme its credibility.

right.label: What engineering can honestly say
right.detail: '90% it survives past the outage window; here is what moves the odds.' Planning can act on this — advance, stage spares, derate.

slides.punch: A date is astrology. A band with named drivers is engineering.

slides.title: Stage 8 — the advisory, as it should arrive
slides.subtitle: Not an alarm: a claim, with its evidence attached
slides.notes: [14:40–14:43] This is what lands on the desk — walk it top to bottom. The claim, the residual behind it, the mechanism hypothesis, the confirming second witness, the RUL band, and the recommended action with its window. Everything is inspectable; nothing says 'the AI decided'. An advisory in this form respects the engineer who receives it, and that respect — more than any accuracy number — is what decides whether the programme survives its first year.

slides.title: The decomposition that changes the conversation
slides.subtitle: Gross HR = net HR × (1 − aux): split the gap before prescribing the medicine
slides.notes: [15:12–15:16] The most important arithmetic of the block. Net heat rate already CONTAINS auxiliary power, so decompose before diagnosing: our gross heat-rate gap is 176 kcal/kWh — ₹22.87 crore in June — a genuine boiler-turbine thermodynamic shortfall. The auxiliary excess is 0.95 points — ₹3.01 crore — a separate, smaller, electrical-side problem. Nashik, for contrast, is the exact mirror: turbine BEATING norm, entire penalty in aux. Different disease, different medicine — and any AI effort here must be pointed at the thermodynamic gap, because that is where our money is.

Anyone who quotes 'nearly ₹29 crore of addressable loss' has invented several crore a month out of double counting — and will be found out in front of a regulator.

slides.title: Combustion is a trade-off, not a setting
slides.subtitle: SIM-6's surfaces: excess O₂ against heat rate and NOx, from the model itself
slides.notes: [15:50–15:54] The two curves are computed from SIM-6's own model: NOx rises roughly 78 mg/Nm³ per point of excess O₂; heat rate is U-shaped — dry-gas loss punishes high O₂, CO and unburnt carbon punish starving it. There is no single best point, only a frontier of defensible ones, and where you stand on it is POLICY: emissions posture, coal cost, unit condition. That is why the lab next door is multi-objective — and why 'the optimiser says' is never a complete sentence.

OFA, tilt and bias move the frontier itself — that is the optimiser's job
slides.punch: 'The optimiser says' is not a complete sentence. Weights are policy; policy is yours.

slides.subtitle: Eight minutes on the Pareto frontier
slides.notes: [LAB] [15:54–16:02] Short and pointed. Everyone sets the three weights — heat rate, NOx, unburnt carbon — and watches the recommended operating point move along the frontier. The two mandatory experiments: all-weight-on-heat-rate (watch NOx climb toward its limit) and all-weight-on-NOx (watch heat rate pay for it). Close the lab with the deployment sentence: in real plants this arrives as an ADVISORY — setpoint nudges with reasons — and closed-loop only ever follows years of trusted advisory operation.

slides.title: The missing instrument — soft sensors
slides.subtitle: SIM-4 in one slide: coal quality every minute instead of every shift
slides.notes: [16:04–16:06] One breath on SIM-4, because every optimiser upstream depends on it: the lab GCV arrives once a shift, hours late; a soft sensor infers GCV every minute from mill behaviour — feeder rate against heat output, mill power, air temperatures. Our June as-fired GCV averaged 3,061 kcal/kg; the swing WITHIN a day is what the optimisers never see without this. Homework lab, and the natural third pilot behind the two in Block 7.

right.label: Soft-sensor GCV

slides.title: A camera is a very wide sensor
slides.subtitle: The modest, true proposition for vision in a plant
slides.notes: [16:10–16:12] Reset expectations at the door: computer vision does nothing a good engineer cannot do. It does what a good engineer cannot do a hundred times a day, every day, without getting bored. That is the whole proposition — modest, and true, and it survives contact with reality, which grander claims do not. Then the bridge: everything the morning taught about models applies unchanged; only the sensor got wider.

left.detail: Expert, contextual, accountable — and finite. Rounds happen once a shift, attention is scarce, fatigue is real.

right.label: A camera, all day
right.detail: The same simple check — repeated relentlessly, in heat and dust and at 03:00, without boredom. Volume, not brilliance.

slides.title: How a vision model learns
slides.subtitle: The same story as this morning — pixels in, backprop underneath
slides.notes: [16:12–16:15] Demystify by reuse: a vision model is the Theatre's network with a million times more dials and pixels for inputs. The one new idea is convolution — a small filter slid across the image, the same few weights reused everywhere, so the network learns 'edge' and 'helmet-curve' once rather than per-pixel. Everything else — forward pass, error, backprop, training windows, contamination — the room ALREADY knows. Say that explicitly; it is why the morning came first.
steps: Pixels in
An image is a grid of numbers — brightness per pixel. Nothing more exotic enters.
Convolution
A small filter slides over the grid, reusing its weights — learns 'edge' once, finds it everywhere.
Same forward pass
Layers, bends, an output: helmet / no-helmet with a confidence. The Theatre's story, scaled.
Same backprop
Blame shared by the chain rule across millions of dials. Same rule, same risks, same windows.
slides.punch: You already learned vision this morning. Only the sensor got wider.

slides.title: What a vision model needs from you
slides.subtitle: The dataset is the project — again — plus glass that stays clean
slides.notes: [16:15–16:18] The historian lesson repeats with a lens on it. Labelled images by the thousand, lighting that stays consistent, cameras maintained in a plant that coats everything in coal dust, and retraining when anything changes — uniforms, camera angle, season. A dusty lens is a data-quality failure exactly like a frozen sensor: stage 4 of Block 4, for pixels. The 'never' line matters most and sets up SafetyNet's design next.
warnings: Labelled data
Thousands of annotated images per class, covering YOUR site's conditions — not stock photos of clean workers.
Lighting & angle
A model trained on day shots misses night. Move the camera 2 metres and precision quietly falls.
Lens maintenance
Coal dust on glass is a frozen sensor. Camera cleaning is now an instrument-maintenance route.
Domain shift
New uniforms, new season, new contractor PPE colours — retrain triggers, exactly like after an overhaul.
Honest metrics
Precision AND recall, on your own footage, per class — not a vendor's demo reel.
slides.never: Never point a first vision project at: face identification · discipline · protection systems · anything that names a worker

slides.title: Live — SafetyNet
slides.subtitle: A PPE model trained by an engineer at this station, run in front of the room
slides.notes: [LAB] [16:18–16:28] Your model, your demo — the strongest ten minutes of the block. Setup, BEFORE the session: on the laptop, `pip install gradio` and run `python service/gradio_app.py` from the SafetyNet repo — the 19 MB model auto-downloads on first use, so do that first run on hotel or home Wi-Fi, not in the hall. It serves on localhost; no internet needed during the demo itself. Keep 4–5 plant-style photos in a folder ready, and one pre-run Batch-tab CSV as backup if the live run misbehaves — and if it misbehaves anyway, teach from the failure. In the room: use the Image tab; detections appear alongside PER-WORKER verdicts, deliberately side by side so the room can tell a detector miss from a policy decision. Say what it is: YOLO11s, 120 epochs on a free Colab T4 in ~90 minutes, 2,801 images, 10 classes, 19 MB — trained by an Assistant Engineer with zero procurement.

slides.title: The question nobody's dataset answers
slides.subtitle: From 'is there a hardhat in this image?' to 'is THAT worker wearing one?'
slides.notes: [16:28–16:31] The dataset labels PPE as independent boxes, so a detector alone answers a question nobody asked. The site's question is attribution — whose hardhat is that? — and bridging the two is where SafetyNet's real engineering lives: three priors combined — containment, anatomical position, and SCALE, because a worker 30 metres away stands 'inside' the box of a worker 3 metres away, and containment alone happily awards the near worker the far worker's helmet. This is feature engineering, Block 4 stage 5, in pixels — and mAP cannot measure any of it.
steps: Detect
10-class YOLO finds people and PPE as independent boxes. The only GPU stage.
Attribute
Each PPE box matched to at most one worker: containment × anatomy × scale, as a soft AND.
Judge
Site policy decides what the attribution means — including an honest UNKNOWN.
Debounce
A violation must persist across frames before it becomes an event. One event, not 400 frames.
slides.punch: mAP measures the detector. The site's question is answered two stages later — measure THOSE.

slides.title: SafetyNet's honest numbers
slides.subtitle: What it measures, what it misses, what it refuses to guess
slides.notes: [16:31–16:34] Put the metrics up without varnish. mAP50 0.852, precision 0.921 — when it flags, it is right nine times in ten. Recall 0.787 — it MISSES one violation in five, and anyone deploying it must know that number. Then the design choices that make it deployable: below 64 pixels of worker it returns UNKNOWN rather than guessing; when Hardhat and NO-Hardhat fire on the same head within a 0.10 margin, UNKNOWN again. Absence of evidence is not evidence of a violation — systems that skip abstention get switched off in week two.

slides.title: The industrial-relations question
slides.subtitle: Safety system or disciplinary system? Decided by the FIRST alert
slides.notes: [16:36–16:38] The make-or-break slide, and it is not technical. Unions will reasonably ask which system this is, and the answer is settled by what the first alert produces: if it is a show-cause notice against a named individual, the programme is finished, permanently, on day one. The design answer: zone-level statistics, no identification, no name-and-shame, the union briefed BEFORE the first camera — and recall of 0.787 quoted aloud, because a false alert against a named person is a grievance with the programme's name on it.
warnings: Name-and-shame
The first individually-targeted alert converts a safety tool into a surveillance grievance. Permanently.
False accusation
At 0.921 precision, 1 flag in 13 is wrong. Against a named worker, that is a formal grievance waiting.
Discipline creep
If HR ever asks for the footage, the safety framing is dead — and so is the data source.
Union sequencing
Briefed first, with the miss-rate on the table, unions often support zone-level safety statistics.
Metric theatre
Zone compliance trending up may mean PPE improved — or workers learned the camera positions. Audit on foot.

slides.subtitle: Ranked honestly — thermal before optical, statistics before individuals

The course recommendation for a first project is drone stockpile volumetrics: outdoor, uncontroversial, safety-positive, and it produces a number finance already understands.

slides.subtitle: Vision and tags, corroborating — the day's discipline, unified

slides.title: The other half of plant knowledge
slides.subtitle: The historian holds the numbers. The documents hold everything else.
slides.notes: [16:40–16:42] Pivot fast — twenty minutes left, three slides of GenAI, then decisions. The plant's other knowledge base: manuals, SOPs, log books, trip reports, OEM letters — none of it in the historian, most of it findable only through one retiring engineer's memory. A language model alone knows NONE of our documents and will answer questions about them confidently anyway; fluent wrongness near a permit-to-work is worse than no answer. The fix is not a bigger model — it is grounding.

left.label: What an LLM is
left.detail: Trained on public text. It contains none of our SOPs, limits or revisions — and no signal for when it is guessing.

right.label: The danger mode
right.detail: A confident, well-phrased answer citing nothing. Near a PTW or an OEM limit, fluency without provenance is a hazard.

slides.punch: The failure mode is not gibberish — it is confidence. Grounding, not size, is the fix.

slides.title: RAG — the answer must quote our document
slides.subtitle: Retrieve first, answer second, cite always
slides.notes: [16:42–16:45] RAG in four steps, no mystique: chunk our documents, index them by meaning, retrieve the passages relevant to the question, and answer FROM those passages with document, revision and page attached to every claim. If nothing relevant is retrieved, say so — that is a feature. The practical lever, measured on the session's own bench: metadata. Clean section titles and revision tags moved recall from 84 to 90 percent — document hygiene, an AE-controllable input, beat the choice of model. The trust checklist: citation present, document current, numbers recomputed.
steps: Chunk & index
Split manuals and SOPs into passages; index by meaning, tagged with document, revision, page.
Retrieve
The question finds its passages first — recall@5 of 90% hybrid on the session's measured bench.
Answer, grounded
The model writes ONLY from what was retrieved. Nothing retrieved → 'not found', honestly.
Cite
Document, revision, page on every claim. Trust check: citation present · doc current · numbers recomputed.
slides.punch: Metadata beat the model: titles and revisions moved recall more than any algorithm choice.
